title: Health ministry study: richer groups now gain most from public hospital care
excerpt: A Health Economics Unit study found the poorest 40% got 33% of public inpatient benefits in 2022, down from 46% in 2016. Health costs pushed 1.08 crore people into poverty.

image.alt: File photo: a hospital building on a busy street in Dhaka
image.credit: File photo: Rashed Ali / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

content:
Wealthier Bangladeshis now get a larger share of the benefits of public hospital inpatient care than the poor, according to a study by the health ministry's Health Economics Unit (HEU), The Daily Star reported on Wednesday (25 November). The study was carried out with support from the World Health Organization and the Swedish Embassy, and its findings were presented last month, the paper said.

The study analysed four rounds of the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (2005, 2010, 2016 and 2022). In 2016, the poorest two of five wealth groups received 46% of the benefits from public inpatient services, against 28% for the richest two. By 2022 this had reversed: 33% for the poorest two groups and 38% for the richest. In outpatient care, the richest two groups kept the larger share, 44% in 2022 against 37% for the poorest.

The share of people facing financial hardship from out-of-pocket health spending rose from 28.2% in 2005 to 41.7% in 2022. In 2022, 90.8% of people in the poorest consumption group faced such hardship, compared with 13.6% in the richest. Out-of-pocket costs pushed more than 1.08 crore people below the poverty line in 2022, almost double the 56 lakh in 2005. The share of people going to pharmacies for outpatient treatment rose from 32.5% in 2016 to 55.4% in 2022. The report recommended restoring a pro-poor distribution of public health benefits.

Subrata Paul, the HEU's focal point for universal health coverage and National Health Accounts, told The Daily Star that big cities lack public primary and secondary facilities, so patients rely on tertiary government hospitals, and that rising household costs are making private care hard to afford even for better-off families. Prof Be-Nazir Ahmed, former director of disease control at the DGHS, said politically connected people and local elites often get better access to public services.

State Minister for Health MA Muhit blamed the previous Awami League government for years of mismanagement and neglect, The Daily Star reported. He said the current government "could neither take credit nor responsibility for the findings" and asked researchers to carry out a rapid assessment in 2026 as a baseline.

Why it matters

The government's share of total health spending fell from 17% in 1997 to 10% in 2020, according to the National Health Accounts, The Daily Star reported. If public hospitals are serving richer patients, the poorest are left with pharmacies and private costs. NGOs running health financing, social protection and community health schemes can use these figures to press for better targeting of public services in cities.

What to watch

Whether the health ministry publishes the full HEU report, acts on its recommendations, and commissions the 2026 baseline assessment the state minister requested. Devlens has not seen the full report and relied on The Daily Star's account.
